line: National-defense information and the classified-documents record (Mar-a-Lago prosecution; 2017/2019 disclosure episodes; 2025-2026 handling of classified material). This is the closest the record comes to the offence family people mean by 'treason' - and it is not treason. It is 18 U.S.C. 793(e), an Espionage Act retention offence, plus obstruction. No count in any indictment, and no clause at issue in any filing, is Article III Section 3.

findings.claim: A federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida returned a superseding indictment on 27 July 2023 in United States v. Trump, Nauta and De Oliveira, No. 23-CR-80101-CANNON(s), charging 40 counts in total. Counts 1-32 charge DONALD J. TRUMP alone with Willful Retention of National Defense Information under 18 U.S.C. 793(e) - one count per document. Counts 33-38 and 40 charge obstruction and false-statement offences: Count 33 conspiracy to obstruct justice (18 U.S.C. 1512(k), all three defendants); Count 34 withholding a document or record (1512(b)(2)(A) and 2, Trump and Nauta); Count 35 corruptly concealing a document or record (1512(c)(1) and 2, Trump and Nauta); Count 36 concealing a document in a federal investigation (1519 and 2 - the caption page did not extract from the scanned copy, but 1519 appears in the indictment's statute header and nowhere else); Count 37 scheme to conceal (1001(a)(1) and 2, Trump and Nauta); Count 38 false statements and representations (1001(a)(2) and 2, Trump alone, as to the 3 June 2022 certification); Count 40 altering, destroying, mutilating or concealing an object (1512(b)(2)(B) and 2, all three defendants). Count 39 (1001(a)(2)) charges Nauta alone.
findings.legal_frame: 18 U.S.C. 793(e) (willful retention of national defense information); 18 U.S.C. 1512(k), 1512(b)(2)(A), 1512(b)(2)(B), 1512(c)(1); 18 U.S.C. 1519; 18 U.S.C. 1001(a)(1), 1001(a)(2); 18 U.S.C. 2 (aiding and abetting)
sources: Superseding Indictment, United States v. Trump, Nauta and De Oliveira, No. 23-CR-80101-CANNON(s) (S.D. Fla. 27 July 2023), 60 pp., text extracted from the scanned copy at https://media.arkansasonline.com/news/documents/2023/07/27/us-v-trump-nauta-de-oliveira.pdf (fetched 7 Sept 2026; the DOJ-hosted copy at https://www.justice.gov/storage/US-v-Trump-Nauta-De-Oliveira-23-80101.pdf returned an HTML interstitial, not the PDF)

CourtListener docket, United States v. Trump, 9:23-cr-80101 (S.D. Fla.), https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/67490070/united-states-v-trump/ (HTTP 403 on fetch; listed for the docket identity only, not relied on for content)
findings.establishes: That a grand jury found probable cause on 32 counts of willful retention of national defense information and seven obstruction/false-statement counts against Trump, and the exact statutes charged. Probable cause, no more.
findings.does_not: Establish guilt of anything. No count went to trial. No jury verdict exists. It does not establish that any document was transmitted to, or reached, any foreign power - no count under 18 U.S.C. 794 or 798 was brought. It is not an adjudication of any kind.
findings.counter_record: An indictment is an accusation only. Trump pleaded not guilty on all counts (arraignments 13 June and 10 Aug 2023). The entire superseding indictment was dismissed on 15 July 2024 (see CD-06) and never reinstated. On the face of the document Trump is named in 39 of the 40 counts, not 40 - Count 39 charges Nauta alone - although the district court's own dismissal order and most contemporaneous reporting describe it as a '40-count' indictment against Trump. I flag the discrepancy rather than resolve it: Count 36's caption did not extract from the scanned copy available to me.
findings.status: charged, then dismissed - not on the merits (see CD-06, CD-07)
findings.notes: The indictment's General Allegations define the markings at issue: TOP SECRET / SECRET / CONFIDENTIAL, NOFORN ('Not Releasable to Foreign Nationals'), SCI (Sensitive Compartmented Information, requiring a SCIF), and SAP (Special Access Programs). The Counts 1-32 table itself is a scanned table that did not extract; one legible fragment reads 'TOP SECRET//SPECIAL HANDLING' and another 'Document dated June 4, 2020, concerning White House intelligence briefing... to various foreign countries'. I did not reconstruct the per-count marking list and do not assert one.

findings.claim: The superseding indictment alleges, at General Allegation 8, that classified documents were recovered from Trump in three tranches in 2022: (a) 17 January 2022 - Trump provided NARA 15 boxes containing 197 documents with classification markings; (b) 3 June 2022 - in response to the 11 May 2022 grand jury subpoena, Trump's attorney provided the FBI 38 more documents with classification markings; (c) 8 August 2022 - under a court-authorised search warrant, the FBI seized 102 more documents with classification markings, broken down as: Trump's office 27 (6 Top Secret, 18 Secret, 3 Confidential) and the Storage Room 75 (11 Top Secret, 36 Secret, 28 Confidential).
findings.legal_frame: 18 U.S.C. 793(e); 44 U.S.C. 2201-2209 (Presidential Records Act, civil, no criminal penalty)
sources: Superseding Indictment, paras. 8, 65, 89-90, No. 23-CR-80101-CANNON(s) (S.D. Fla. 27 July 2023), https://media.arkansasonline.com/news/documents/2023/07/27/us-v-trump-nauta-de-oliveira.pdf
findings.establishes: The government's alleged counts and marking breakdown of documents recovered, and that the 8 Aug 2022 seizure followed a court-authorised warrant (i.e. a judge found probable cause).
findings.does_not: Establish that every marked document was in fact currently classified, or that every marked document was 'information relating to the national defense' within 793(e) - those are trial issues that were never tried. Marking is evidence of national-defense character; it is not the element.
findings.counter_record: Only 32 documents - not 337 - were charged under 793(e). The government itself declined to charge on the overwhelming majority of the marked documents recovered, which is the strongest available indication that marking alone did not satisfy the prosecutors' own charging standard. Trump's public position throughout was that he had declassified the material and that the Presidential Records Act made the documents his personal records (rejected as a matter of law, see CD-15).
findings.status: alleged in a dismissed indictment; never adjudicated
findings.notes: The 15-box / 197-document January 2022 tranche is the NARA referral that generated the FBI investigation opened 30 March 2022 (General Allegation 7).

findings.claim: General Allegation 6(a): 'In July 2021, at Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey ... during an audio-recorded meeting with a writer, a publisher, and two members of his staff, none of whom possessed a security clearance, TRUMP showed and described a "plan of attack" that TRUMP said was prepared for him by the Department of Defense and a senior military official. TRUMP told the individuals that the plan was "highly confidential" and "secret." TRUMP also said, "as president I could have declassified it" and, "Now I can't, you know, but this is still a secret."' The recording was made for work on Mark Meadows' memoir; CNN obtained and published the audio on 26 June 2023. The document referenced concerned a potential attack on Iran. The superseding indictment added this document as a 793(e) count (Count 32).
findings.legal_frame: 18 U.S.C. 793(e) - willful retention. Note: showing a document to an uncleared person is charged here only as evidence of retention and of knowledge that the material remained classified; no transmission count (793(d), 794, 798) was brought.
sources: Superseding Indictment, General Allegation 6(a), No. 23-CR-80101-CANNON(s) (S.D. Fla. 27 July 2023), https://media.arkansasonline.com/news/documents/2023/07/27/us-v-trump-nauta-de-oliveira.pdf
CNN, 'Exclusive: CNN obtains the tape of Trump's 2021 conversation about classified documents', 26 June 2023, https://www.cnn.com/2023/06/26/politics/trump-classified-documents-audio
CNN, 'What we know about the document Trump mentioned in the taped Bedminster meeting', 28 June 2023, https://www.cnn.com/2023/06/28/politics/trump-bedminster-document
Axios, 'Trump charged with retaining classified document he bragged about on tape', 27 July 2023, https://www.axios.com/2023/07/27/trump-additional-charges-classified-documents-bedminster-recording
findings.establishes: That a contemporaneous audio recording exists in which Trump, after leaving office, describes a document in his possession as still secret and says he could have declassified it as president but can no longer do so. That statement is the government's answer to the standing declassification defence, in Trump's own recorded words.
findings.does_not: Establish that the object he was holding was in fact the DoD document, or that it was in fact classified, or that anyone read it. It does not establish transmission to a foreign power or intent to injure the United States - neither was charged.
findings.counter_record: The specific Iran document referenced on the tape was never recovered. Trump's team searched and told the government it could not locate it. Trump's own account (Fox News, June 2023): 'There was no document. That was a massive amount of papers and everything else talking about Iran and other things ... I didn't have a document, per se. There was nothing to declassify. These were newspaper stories, magazine stories and articles.' The audio is in tension with that account but does not by itself identify the object. The count was never tried.
findings.status: charged as Count 32; dismissed with the whole indictment 15 July 2024; never tried
findings.notes: The government never recovered the document. That null is part of the record and cuts against the count.

findings.claim: General Allegation 6(b): 'In August or September 2021, at The Bedminster Club, TRUMP showed a representative of his political action committee who did not possess a security clearance a classified map related to a military operation and told the representative that he should not be showing it to the representative and that the representative should not get too close.'
findings.legal_frame: 18 U.S.C. 793(e) (offered as evidence of retention and consciousness of classification status). No 793(d) transmission count was charged as to this episode.
sources: Superseding Indictment, General Allegation 6(b), No. 23-CR-80101-CANNON(s) (S.D. Fla. 27 July 2023), https://media.arkansasonline.com/news/documents/2023/07/27/us-v-trump-nauta-de-oliveira.pdf
findings.establishes: That the grand jury found probable cause for a second post-presidency showing of classified material to an uncleared person, and that Trump's own contemporaneous words as alleged show awareness that he should not be doing it.
findings.does_not: Identify the map, the operation, or the PAC representative. It does not establish that the representative saw or retained anything, or that the map reached any third party.
findings.counter_record: Searched: no public denial, alternative account, or defence filing specifically addressing this allegation was located. The allegation was never tested at trial and the PAC representative is not named in the indictment. Note also the anti-map guardrail: this episode and the June 2022 plane-map allegation in CD-10 are separate reported events and are not established to be the same map or the same document.
findings.status: alleged in a dismissed indictment; never adjudicated
findings.notes: Not charged as its own count.

findings.claim: Multiple US outlets reported in October 2023 that Anthony Pratt, an Australian packaging billionaire and Mar-a-Lago member, told associates that at an April 2021 meeting at Mar-a-Lago Trump described two items about US nuclear submarines: the number of nuclear warheads they routinely carry, and how close they can get to a Russian submarine without detection. Pratt was reported to have been interviewed by the Special Counsel's office and to be a potential trial witness. Pratt was reported to have repeated the account to roughly 45 people, including journalists, Pratt Industries employees, Australian officials and three former Australian prime ministers.
findings.legal_frame: none charged. Had a transmission theory been pursued it would have run to 18 U.S.C. 793(d) or, for atomic-energy/Restricted Data, 42 U.S.C. 2274 - neither was brought. No count in either indictment references this episode.
sources: ABC News, 'Trump allegedly discussed US nuclear subs with foreign national after leaving White House: Sources', 5 Oct 2023, https://abcnews.com/US/after-white-house-trump-allegedly-discussed-potentially-sensitive/story?id=103760456

CNN, 'ABC: Trump allegedly discussed sensitive nuclear submarine information with a Mar-a-Lago member', 5 Oct 2023, https://www.cnn.com/2023/10/05/politics/trump-nuclear-information-australian-billionaire/index.html

CBS News, 'Trump discussed nuclear submarines with Australian billionaire Anthony Pratt, three sources say', Oct 2023, https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-nuclear-submarines-australian-billionaire-anthony-pratt/
findings.establishes: That reporting sourced to people familiar with the investigation described this account and Pratt's witness status. Nothing more.
findings.does_not: Establish that the conversation happened as described, that anything said was accurate, that anything said was classified, or that any document changed hands. Reporting expressly stated there was no indication Trump shared any records with Pratt. It establishes nothing about Pratt, who is not accused of wrongdoing.
findings.counter_record: This episode appears nowhere in the original or superseding indictment. The prosecutors who had Pratt's account and could have charged a transmission count did not charge one. Under the symmetry rule that is the single most important fact here and it cuts against the allegation. Trump's spokesman called the reporting part of a politically motivated campaign. The account is hearsay-of-hearsay: sources describing what Pratt told others about what Trump told him.
findings.status: never charged; investigation closed with the case
findings.notes: The brief asked for 'the Australian businessman'. He is not in the indictment. Holding him at 'labeled' is the correct tier and the gap between the reporting and the charging decision is the finding.

findings.claim: On 15 July 2024 Judge Aileen M. Cannon (S.D. Fla.) granted Trump's motion to dismiss and entered an 'Order Granting Motion to Dismiss Superseding Indictment Based on Appointments Clause Violation' (93 pp.): 'The Superseding Indictment is DISMISSED because Special Counsel Smith's appointment violates the Appointments Clause of the United States Constitution.' The order further held that 'Special Counsel Smith's use of a permanent indefinite appropriation also violates the Appropriations Clause,' but declined to reach a remedy for the funding violation given the Appointments Clause dismissal, and stated that 'the effect of this Order is confined to this proceeding.'
findings.legal_frame: U.S. Const. art. II, sec. 2, cl. 2 (Appointments Clause); U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 9, cl. 7 (Appropriations Clause); 28 U.S.C. 515, 533 (the appointment authorities the court held insufficient)
sources: United States v. Trump, No. 23-80101-CR-CANNON (S.D. Fla. 15 July 2024), order text reproduced at FindLaw, https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-dis-crt-s-d-flo-wes-pal-bea-div/116378544.html
Lawfare, 'Judge Cannon Dismisses Trump Classified Documents Case', 15 July 2024, https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/judge-cannon-dismisses-trump-classified-documents-case
Just Security, 'Judge Cannon Finds Special Counsel Unconstitutional in Trump Classified Documents Case', 15 July 2024, https://www.justsecurity.org/97747/trump-docs-case-dismissed/
findings.establishes: That the case ended on a structural constitutional defect in who brought it - the appointing officer - and on nothing else.
findings.does_not: Adjudicate a single fact alleged in the indictment. It is not an acquittal, not a finding of innocence, not a finding that the documents were declassified, not a finding that the retention was lawful. Guaranteed-null rule applies in the other direction too: the dismissal is equally consistent with the conduct having occurred and with it not having occurred, and is evidence about neither.
findings.counter_record: The ruling was an outlier: as Smith's office noted, it deviated from the uniform conclusion of every prior court to consider whether the Attorney General may appoint a Special Counsel (including in the Mueller and Hunter Biden matters). It was never affirmed on appeal - the appeal was withdrawn, not decided (CD-07) - so it stands as one district judge's unreviewed holding and creates no binding precedent anywhere. Conversely, its reasoning drew on Justice Thomas's concurrence in Trump v. United States, 603 U.S. 593 (2024).
findings.status: dismissed - not on the merits; appeal taken and then abandoned; never reviewed
findings.notes: I could not confirm the ECF number of the order itself from a primary docket (CourtListener returned 403). Contemporaneous reporting and later filings refer to it as the 15 July 2024 order. I could not confirm from the order text whether the dismissal was with or without prejudice; an Appointments Clause dismissal ordinarily does not bar re-indictment by a properly appointed officer, and I state no conclusion.

findings.claim: The case was never revived. Smith noticed an appeal to the Eleventh Circuit and filed his opening brief on 26 Aug 2024. On 25 November 2024, after the election, Smith moved to dismiss the charges against Trump citing the Office of Legal Counsel's longstanding opinion that a sitting President may not be prosecuted; the Eleventh Circuit dropped Trump from the appeal on 26 November 2024. Smith continued the appeal as to Nauta and De Oliveira only. On 29 January 2025 the Trump Justice Department moved unopposed to dismiss that remaining appeal, and on 11 February 2025 the Eleventh Circuit dismissed it, ending the prosecution as to all three defendants. No pardons were issued in this case.
findings.legal_frame: OLC, 'A Sitting President's Amenability to Indictment and Criminal Prosecution' (2000) - executive-branch policy, not a judicial holding; Fed. R. Crim. P. 48(a)
sources: NPR, 'Special counsel Jack Smith appeals ruling tossing Trump's classified documents case', 26 Aug 2024, https://www.npr.org/2024/08/26/g-s1-19642/special-counsel-jack-smith-judge-cannon-appeal-trump-classified-documents

CNN, 'Special counsel Jack Smith drops election subversion and classified documents cases against Donald Trump', 25 Nov 2024, https://www.cnn.com/2024/11/25/politics/trump-special-counsel-jack-smith/index.html

NBC News, 'Appeals court agrees to dismiss Trump's classified documents case', 26 Nov 2024, https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/appeals-court-agrees-dismiss-trumps-classified-documents-case-rcna181942
NPR, 'DOJ asks to dismiss case of 2 men indicted for allegedly helping Trump hide documents', 29 Jan 2025, https://www.npr.org/2025/01/29/nx-s1-5279387/doj-appeal-trump-walt-nauta-carlos-de-oliveira
NPR, 'Court drops remaining classified documents appeal against Trump's aides', 11 Feb 2025, https://www.npr.org/2025/02/11/nx-s1-5293113/trump-document-case-nauta-de-oliveira
findings.establishes: That the prosecution terminated through (i) a district-court structural ruling, (ii) an executive-branch policy against prosecuting a sitting President, and (iii) a discretionary dismissal by the succeeding administration - three exits, none of them a merits determination.
findings.does_not: Establish anything at all about whether the conduct occurred. This is the guaranteed-null rule in its purest form on this line: the same outcome - no adjudication - follows whether Trump was guilty, innocent, or somewhere between. Nobody should read the ending of this case in either direction.
findings.counter_record: The dismissal as to Trump was expressly without prejudice - the OLC bar is temporary and coextensive with his tenure, and Smith's filing said so. That is a live fact against reading the dismissal as vindication. Cutting the other way: the current Justice Department is a party in interest to the defendant's favour, and the 2025 abandonment of the co-defendants' appeal was a discretionary choice by an administration the defendants serve. Notably, no pardon was issued to Nauta or De Oliveira - reportedly because a pardon implies wrongdoing to forgive - so the pardon-as-null question does not arise here.
findings.status: dismissed on DOJ policy (Trump) and on prosecutorial discretion (co-defendants); no merits ruling; no conviction; no acquittal; no pardon
findings.notes: Charges against Trump could in principle be re-brought after 20 January 2029, subject to the statute of limitations (5 years under 18 U.S.C. 3282 for these offences, which for most counts would have run before then absent tolling). I did not research tolling and make no claim about revivability.

findings.claim: Special Counsel Smith's final report was delivered to the Attorney General in two volumes on 7 January 2025. Volume I (election-interference case, 137 pp.) was transmitted to Congress and released publicly on 14 January 2025, and stated: 'But for Mr. Trump's election and imminent return to the Presidency, the Office assessed that the admissible evidence was sufficient to obtain and sustain a conviction at trial.' Volume II (the classified-documents case) has never been released. Judge Cannon enjoined its release on 21 January 2025 while the co-defendants' appeal was pending. After that appeal was dismissed, the injunction persisted; on 3 November 2025 the Eleventh Circuit found her delay in ruling on the Knight First Amendment Institute's access motion 'undue' and ordered her to resolve it within 60 days; she denied the motion 11 days before that deadline. On 23 February 2026 she entered an order (United States v. Trump, S.D. Fla., ECF No. 779) permanently blocking release of Volume II and confirming that the June 2023 Rule 16 protective order (ECF No. 27) remains in effect without change. Appeals by American Oversight and the Knight Institute are pending in the Eleventh Circuit; the Knight Institute filed a supplemental opening brief on 11 June 2026. No Eleventh Circuit merits ruling had issued as of 7 September 2026.
findings.legal_frame: 28 C.F.R. 600.8(c) (Special Counsel final report); Fed. R. Crim. P. 16(d) (protective order); Fed. R. Crim. P. 6(e) (grand jury secrecy); First Amendment and common-law right of access (the intervenors' theory)
sources: Statement of Jack Smith, Former Special Counsel, before the House Committee on the Judiciary, 22 January 2026, 3 pp., https://judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/republicans-judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/smith-testimony.pdf (fetched and text-extracted)

Letter, Rep. Jamie Raskin to Attorney General Pamela Bondi, 24 March 2026, 6 pp., nn. 2 and 5 (citing United States v. Trump, No. 9:23-cr-80101-AMC (S.D. Fla.), ECF No. 27 (19 June 2023) and ECF No. 779 (23 Feb. 2026)), https://democrats-judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/2026-03-24-raskin-to-bondi-doj-re-classified-docs.pdf (fetched and text-extracted)

American Oversight, 'American Oversight Condemns Judge Cannon's Order Permanently Blocking Release of Volume II of Jack Smith Report', https://americanoversight.org/american-oversight-condemns-judge-cannons-order-permanently-blocking-release-of-volume-ii-of-jack-smith-report/

American Oversight, 'Appeals Court Presses Judge Aileen Cannon to Address Delay in Special Counsel Report Case', https://americanoversight.org/appeals-court-presses-judge-aileen-cannon-to-release-jack-smith-report-volume-two/

CBS News, 'Special counsel's final report says Trump would have been convicted of election interference if he hadn't won', 14 Jan 2025, https://www.cbsnews.com/news/special-counsel-report-trump-partially-released/
Yale Law School, 'Clinic Urges 11th Circuit to Unseal Special Counsel Jack Smith's Report', https://law.yale.edu/yls-today/news/clinic-urges-11th-circuit-unseal-special-counsel-jack-smiths-report
findings.establishes: That the prosecutor's own written account of the documents investigation exists, is complete, and is under a judicial seal that has now been made permanent by the same judge who dismissed the case; and that the seal has been repeatedly contested and once found unduly delayed by the court of appeals.
findings.does_not: Establish what Volume II says. Guaranteed-null rule, stated at full strength: the suppression of Volume II is evidence of nothing about its contents. It is equally consistent with a damning document, an exculpatory one, and an unremarkable one. Anyone - in either direction - who reads the seal as a signal about the underlying conduct is reasoning from a test that cannot come out against them.
findings.counter_record: The stated legal grounds are not frivolous: while the co-defendants' appeal was live, releasing a prosecutor's narrative of the case against them raised a real fair-trial problem, and DOJ's own position was that a Rule 6(e) review is no longer feasible because the Special Counsel's team has left the Department. America First Legal has urged the Eleventh Circuit to go further and order the report destroyed as the product of an unconstitutional appointment - a position that follows logically from Cannon's July 2024 holding. Against that: the co-defendants' appeal ended on 11 February 2025 and the seal outlived it by more than a year.
findings.status: under appeal; Volume II sealed; no merits ruling from the Eleventh Circuit located as of 7 Sept 2026
findings.notes: Volume I is public and is about the election case, not this line. I have not read Volume II and no one outside a small circle has.

findings.claim: In his written statement to the House Judiciary Committee dated 22 January 2026, Smith stated under his own name: 'as set forth in the original and superseding indictments issued in the Southern District of Florida, President Trump stored classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago social club after he left office in January 2021 and he repeatedly tried to obstruct justice to conceal his continued retention of those documents. Highly sensitive information was held in non-secure locations, including a bathroom and a ballroom where events and gatherings took place. Tens of thousands of people came to the social club during the time period when those classified documents were stored there.' He added: 'Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in criminal activity,' and stated that he was 'constrained by Judge Cannon's order restricting the discussion of Volume II' and 'will not be able to discuss the contents of Volume II ... and can only discuss matters with respect to that case that are set forth in the indictment or other public filings.' He had earlier testified in closed session for over eight hours on 17 December 2025; the Committee released 255 pages of that transcript and the video on 31 December 2025.
findings.legal_frame: none - sworn congressional testimony by the former prosecutor; not itself a legal finding
sources: Statement of Jack Smith before the House Committee on the Judiciary, 22 January 2026, https://judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/republicans-judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/smith-testimony.pdf (fetched, quoted verbatim)
CNN, 'Jack Smith testifies in closed-door hearing that it was his decision to charge Trump', 17 Dec 2025, https://www.cnn.com/2025/12/17/politics/jack-smith-house-judiciary-committee-testimony

CNN, 'House Judiciary Committee releases video and transcript of Jack Smith deposition on New Year's Eve', 31 Dec 2025, https://www.cnn.com/2025/12/31/politics/jack-smith-house-judiciary-committee-deposition-released
NPR, 'Jack Smith testifies in House over Trump investigations', 22 Jan 2026, https://www.npr.org/2026/01/22/nx-s1-5683973/jack-smith-house-trump-investigations
findings.establishes: That the prosecutor who brought the case has now said in a public, on-the-record congressional appearance that his office had proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and that he is legally barred from saying what is in Volume II.
findings.does_not: Establish guilt. A prosecutor's assessment of his own case is an interested professional judgment, not an adjudication, and it is the same judgment implicit in bringing the indictment. It adds his personal credibility, not a new fact. Under the testimony tier this is evidence of his belief and of the constraint he is under - nothing about the documents themselves.
findings.counter_record: Smith is a contested witness: House Republicans convened the deposition to examine allegations of political motivation in his investigations, and the current Justice Department has publicly disputed his conduct. He is also constrained from producing the underlying material that would allow his claim to be checked, which means the claim is currently unfalsifiable - a fact that should reduce, not increase, its weight. Trump has consistently denied wrongdoing and characterised both prosecutions as politically directed.
findings.notes: The written statement was obtained and extracted directly; the quotations above are verbatim from it.

findings.claim: On 24 March 2026 Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, wrote to Attorney General Pamela Bondi describing a 13 January 2023 prosecution memorandum produced by DOJ to the Committee on 13 March 2026 (Bates DOJ-JSAF-031326-000085 to -000096). Per Raskin, quoting the memo: the FBI determined the retained classified documents 'were commingled with documents created after Trump left office'; certain retained classified documents 'would be pertinent to certain business interests'; prosecutors assessed that 'classified documents pertinent to his business interests' established 'a motive for retaining them. We must have those documents.'; disclosure represented 'an aggravated potential harm to national security'; these were 'highly sensitive documents - the type of documents that only presidents and officials with the most sensitive authority have'; one 'particularly sensitive document was accessible by only 6? people, including the president.' The memo further stated that a then-23-year-old Trump aide, Chamberlain Harris (now Director of Oval Office Operations), 'scanned' the contents of one box onto her laptop, retained it for nearly two years, and 'uploaded the scan to a cloud'; a Trump lawyer retrieved the scan and flew commercially with a thumb drive containing the classified documents, after which the memo is redacted. And: prosecutors 'identified a classified map that we believe Trump may have shown to individuals on board' a 3 June 2022 flight to Bedminster, and their investigation 'indicates that Susan Wiles, the CEO of Trump's Super PAC was aboard that flight and witnessed this event.' Raskin posed eight questions with a 31 March 2026 deadline. DOJ publicly dismissed the letter as a political stunt.
findings.tier: documented as to the existence and contents of the letter and its quotations from a produced DOJ document; the underlying prosecutorial assessments are attributed
findings.legal_frame: 18 U.S.C. 793(e) (the memo is an internal charging assessment in that investigation); Fed. R. Crim. P. 6(e) and the Rule 16 protective order (Raskin's separate allegation that DOJ's own production may have breached both)
sources: Letter, Rep. Jamie Raskin to Attorney General Pamela Bondi, 24 March 2026, 6 pp., https://democrats-judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/2026-03-24-raskin-to-bondi-doj-re-classified-docs.pdf (fetched and text-extracted; all quotations above are verbatim from the letter)
Axios, 'Raskin says Pam Bondi's DOJ gave him "damning" memo on Trump classified docs case', 25 March 2026, https://www.axios.com/2026/03/25/trump-bondi-raskin-doj-classified-documents

Al Jazeera, 'Democrat alleges Trump "sold out" US security in classified documents case', 25 March 2026, https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/25/democrat-alleges-trump-sold-out-us-security-in-classified-documents-case

House Judiciary Committee Democrats, 'Damning New Documents Obtained By Judiciary Democrats Reveal Trump Stole Classified Documents to Advance His Business Interests', https://democrats-judiciary.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/damning-new-documents-obtained-by-judiciary-democrats-reveal-trump-stole-classified-documents-to-advance-his-business-interests
findings.establishes: That an internal prosecution memorandum dated 13 January 2023 exists, that DOJ produced it to Congress in March 2026, and that it contains the quoted prosecutorial assessments - including a stated business-interest motive theory, a six-person-access document, an unsecured scan-and-cloud-upload incident, and an identified June 2022 in-flight map episode witnessed by a named person who is now White House Chief of Staff. It also establishes that DOJ itself put this material into congressional hands.
findings.does_not: Establish that any of the memo's assessments are true. A prosecution memo is an internal argument by advocates at an early stage of an investigation, written to justify investigative steps, not a finding. It does not establish which business interests, which documents, that any document was in fact shown to anyone on the plane, that Wiles saw anything classified, that Chamberlain Harris did anything unlawful, or that any material was compromised - the memo is redacted at exactly that point. It emphatically does not establish that Trump sold, bartered, or traded national defense information to anyone; the memo as quoted asserts a retention motive, not a transaction. Raskin's framing ('may have sold out our national security to enrich himself') is his characterisation, not the memo's language.
findings.counter_record: DOJ's response was that the allegations are baseless and the letter 'a cheap political stunt' by a member 'blinded by hatred of President Trump'. Raskin is the ranking minority member and a political adversary; the letter is advocacy. The material is quoted selectively by him from a production he criticises as itself selective. The eight questions were not, so far as I found, answered. Most importantly: prosecutors who wrote this memo in January 2023 and then indicted in June and July 2023 charged no offence relating to business interests, no transmission, and no foreign recipient - the charging document is the best evidence of what they concluded they could prove, and it contains none of this. The related speculation in the letter about Saudi counterparties (LIV Golf, Dar al Arkan, Yasir al-Rumayyan) is Raskin's inference from public reporting about timing, not anything in the memo. Shared timeline is not a chain.
findings.status: congressional oversight correspondence; never charged; no investigation reopened
findings.notes: Chamberlain Harris and Susie Wiles are living, uncharged persons; the record shows only what the memo as quoted says about them and nothing further should be read into it. The 'business interests' thread is the single most consequential unresolved item on this line, and it is unresolved: the documents at issue are unknown, the interests are unnamed, and the memo is redacted.

findings.claim: On 10 May 2017, in an Oval Office meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Ambassador Sergey Kislyak, Trump discussed intelligence about an ISIS plot to conceal explosives in laptops. The Washington Post reported on 15 May 2017 that the intelligence was codeword-classified, had been provided by a US ally under an arrangement barring onward sharing, and included detail (including the city where the plot was developing) from which the Russians could plausibly deduce the source and the collection method. Subsequent reporting identified the ally as Israel. The White House response shifted over roughly 24 hours: on 15 May then-National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster said the story 'as reported' was false and that at no time were intelligence sources or methods discussed; on 16 May Trump publicly asserted his 'absolute right' to share the information, and McMaster then held a briefing in which he called the conversation 'wholly appropriate,' said 'the president in no way compromised sources or methods,' said no US official present felt the conversation was inappropriate, and said Trump did not know where the information had come from.
findings.tier: documented as to the disclosure occurring and the official statements; contested as to whether classified sources-and-methods information was compromised
findings.legal_frame: None applicable to the President. A sitting President's authority over classification and access to national security information is constitutional and plenary (Department of the Navy v. Egan, 484 U.S. 518, 527 (1988)); E.O. 13526 binds subordinate officials, not the President. There is no criminal statute a President violates by disclosing US classified information to a foreign minister in the Oval Office. The distinct question is whether the disclosure breached a liaison-service control agreement - a diplomatic and intelligence-sharing question, not a criminal one.
sources: Washington Post, 'Trump revealed highly classified information to Russian foreign minister and ambassador', 15 May 2017 (HTTP 403 on direct fetch; content characterised from Wikipedia's sourced summary and contemporaneous secondary reporting, not read directly)
PolitiFact, 'The shifting explanations of Trump's Russia disclosures', 16 May 2017, https://politifact.com/article/2017/may/16/shifting-explanations-trumps-russia-disclosures/

PBS NewsHour, 'President Trump's talk with Russian officials "wholly appropriate," McMaster says', 16 May 2017, https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/president-trumps-talk-russian-officials-wholly-appropriate-mcmaster-says
Foreign Policy, 'Israeli Intelligence Furious Over Trump's Loose Lips', 19 May 2017, https://foreignpolicy.com/2017/05/19/israeli-intelligence-furious-over-trumps-loose-lips-russia-iran-syria/
Wikipedia, 'Donald Trump's disclosures of classified information' (used as an index to the above, not as a citation)
findings.establishes: That the meeting occurred, that Trump himself confirmed sharing 'facts pertaining to terrorism' with the Russian officials, and that the administration's account changed materially within a day. The 16 May defence - 'wholly appropriate' - concedes the disclosure and contests only its propriety, which is itself part of the record.
findings.does_not: Establish that a source, method, or human asset was in fact compromised, that Israel's collection was in fact degraded, or that any law was broken. It does not establish that the disclosure was deliberate rather than careless. No damage assessment has ever been made public.
findings.counter_record: The controlling counter-argument is legal and it is strong: the President is the ultimate classification authority and may disclose US classified information at will (Egan). McMaster, who was in the room, stated on the record that sources and methods were not discussed and that Trump did not know the origin of the information - which if true would make the disclosure inadvertent as to sourcing. Then-Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Deputy NSA Dina Powell both denied that sources, methods or military operations were discussed. Against that: the reporting was that the risk was inferential - the Russians could deduce the source from the detail - which is compatible with McMaster's literal denial that sources were 'discussed'. Both accounts can be true simultaneously; that is why this sits at contested rather than documented on the compromise question. I found no released damage assessment resolving it in either direction.
findings.status: never charged; no criminal statute applicable to a sitting President; no public damage assessment; no investigation known to have been opened
findings.notes: This is the episode most often loosely called 'treason' in public discussion. It is not. Article III treason requires levying war against the United States or adhering to enemies giving them aid and comfort, and 'enemies' in that clause has consistently been read to mean nations or forces with which the United States is in a state of open war. Russia is not one. No prosecutor, no member of Congress in any referral I located, and no court has framed this episode under Article III sec. 3 or 18 U.S.C. 2381.

findings.claim: On 30 August 2019 Trump posted to Twitter a high-resolution annotated overhead image of the aftermath of a failed Safir launch at Iran's Semnan Launch Site One / Imam Khomeini Space Center, with the text that the United States was not involved in the accident. The image carried what appeared to be a black box redacting a classification marking at upper left. Amateur satellite trackers (Marco Langbroek, Netherlands; Michael Thompson, Purdue) reconstructed the imaging time from shadows and geolocation and matched it to the orbit of USA-224, a classified KH-11 ENHANCED CRYSTAL reconnaissance satellite launched by the NRO in 2011. In November 2022, following a FOIA request by NPR, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency formally declassified and released the original image, confirming it had been a classified product.
findings.legal_frame: None applicable to the President; Egan, 484 U.S. at 527, and E.O. 13526 sec. 3.1. A sitting President's public release of an image is itself an act of declassification in substance, whatever the paperwork. The distinct, non-criminal issue is unintended revelation of collection capability (resolution, tasking) - a national-security-management question, not a legal one.
sources: NPR, 'Amateurs Identify U.S. Spy Satellite Behind President Trump's Tweet', 2 Sept 2019, https://www.npr.org/2019/09/02/756673481/amateurs-identify-u-s-spy-satellite-behind-president-trumps-tweet

NPR, 'Trump tweeted an image from a spy satellite, declassified document shows', 18 Nov 2022, https://www.npr.org/2022/11/18/1137474748/trump-tweeted-an-image-from-a-spy-satellite-declassified-document-shows (HTTP 503 on fetch; characterised from search result summary, not read directly)

SatTrackCam Leiden, 'Image from Trump tweet identified as imagery by USA 224, a classified KH-11 ENHANCED CRYSTAL satellite', Sept 2019, https://sattrackcam.blogspot.com/2019/09/image-from-trump-tweet-identified-as.html

The War Zone, 'Trump Tweets Intelligence Image After Iran's Rocket Explosion', 30 Aug 2019, https://www.twz.com/29634/trump-tweets-intelligence-image-after-irans-rocket-explosion-and-offers-them-best-wishes

NPR, 'Trump Tweets Sensitive Surveillance Image Of Iran', 30 Aug 2019, https://www.npr.org/2019/08/30/755994591/president-trump-tweets-sensitive-surveillance-image-of-iran (HTTP 503 on fetch; not read directly)
findings.establishes: That a previously classified NGA imagery product was published by the President on an open platform, and that the publication permitted open-source analysts to identify the specific collection platform and characterise its resolution. The 2022 NGA declassification release is documentary confirmation of the original classification.
findings.does_not: Establish any offence. It does not establish that adversaries learned anything they did not already know - Russia and China track NRO satellites too - and no damage assessment has been published. It does not establish that Trump knew the image was classified or understood the capability implication.
findings.counter_record: The strongest counter is again legal and structural: a sitting President cannot commit an unauthorised disclosure of US classified information by publishing it, and Egan places classification authority in the presidency. The White House position at the time was that the President has the authority to declassify. Analysts including those who did the orbital reconstruction noted the underlying existence and rough capability of KH-11 satellites was long a matter of open-source inference; the tweet sharpened the estimate rather than revealing the program. Against that: the visible redaction box indicates the original bore a classification marking, and no formal declassification action preceded the tweet - the NGA release came three years later and only under FOIA.
findings.status: never charged; no criminal exposure for a sitting President; declassified retroactively by NGA in 2022
findings.notes: The USA-224 attribution is the work of independent trackers, not an official confirmation. I tier that attribution as labeled within an otherwise documented finding; the NGA declassification is documented.

findings.claim: On 15 March 2025 Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth transmitted operational details of imminent US strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen over Signal, a commercial messaging application, from his personal cell phone. The chat had been created by then-National Security Adviser Michael Waltz, who inadvertently added Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg; the roughly 19 participants included Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, DNI Tulsi Gabbard, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and envoy Steve Witkoff. President Trump was not a participant. The DoD Office of Inspector General evaluated the matter from April to October 2025 and published Report No. DODIG-2026-021, 'Evaluation of the Secretary of Defense's Reported Use of a Commercially Available Messaging Application for Official Business' (84 pp., released 2-4 December 2025). The IG found Hegseth 'sent sensitive, nonpublic, operational information' identifying 'the quantity and strike times of manned U.S. aircraft over hostile territory over an unapproved, unsecure network approximately 2 to 4 hours before the execution of those strikes,' that this created operational-security risk that 'could have resulted in failed U.S. mission objectives and potential harm to U.S. pilots,' and that he 'did not comply' with DoD Instruction 8170.01. The report acknowledged Hegseth is an original classification authority and recorded his written position (submitted 25 July 2025, in lieu of an interview) that the details were 'non-specific general details' he determined 'were either not classified or that he could safely declassify.'
findings.legal_frame: DoD Instruction 8170.01 (Online Information Management and Electronic Messaging) - a policy instrument, not a criminal statute. Potentially adjacent: 18 U.S.C. 793(f) (gross negligence in handling national defense information) and 18 U.S.C. 1924 (unauthorized removal/retention of classified material by an officer or employee) - neither was charged, and the IG made no criminal referral I located. Also 44 U.S.C. 2911 and the Federal Records Act as to records retention on ephemeral messaging.
sources: DoD OIG, Report No. DODIG-2026-021, 'Evaluation of the Secretary of Defense's Reported Use of a Commercially Available Messaging Application for Official Business', https://www.dodig.mil/reports.html/Article/4348367/evaluation-of-the-secretary-of-defenses-reported-use-of-a-commercially-availabl/ (landing page located; the report PDF at media.defense.gov returned an HTML interstitial rather than the file, so the report was not read directly)
Lawfare, 'Pentagon Inspector General Releases Report on Hegseth's Signal Use', 4 Dec 2025, https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/pentagon-inspector-general-releases-report-on-hegseth-s-signal-use

Washington Post, 'Watchdog finds Hegseth violated Pentagon protocol in Signalgate affair', 3 Dec 2025, https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2025/12/03/hegseth-signalgate-inspector-general-report/
Just Security, 'Questions Lawmakers Should Ask About Inspector General Report on Signalgate', https://www.justsecurity.org/126591/inspector-general-report-hegseth-signal/
Axios, 'Who was in the Trump administration's explosive Signal group chat', 26 March 2025, https://www.axios.com/2025/03/26/trump-signal-group-chat-members

PBS NewsHour, 'Read the full report on Hegseth's use of Signal from the Pentagon inspector general', https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/read-the-full-report-on-hegseths-use-of-signal-from-the-pentagon-inspector-general
findings.establishes: An official inspector-general finding that the Secretary of Defense transmitted pre-strike operational information about manned US aircraft over hostile territory on an unapproved commercial network, in noncompliance with DoD policy, creating risk to US pilots. It also establishes that a large fraction of the National Security Council principals were conducting operational deliberations on a commercial application.
findings.does_not: Establish that the information was classified - the IG did not so find, and Hegseth held original classification authority over it. It does not establish that any US aircrew was actually harmed or any mission actually failed; the IG expressly said those consequences did not occur. It does not establish any criminal violation, and no charge, referral or discipline followed. Critically for this line, it establishes nothing about President Trump: he was not in the chat.
findings.counter_record: Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell called the report 'a TOTAL exoneration of Secretary Hegseth' and said no classified information was shared; Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker said Hegseth 'acted within his authority.' The IG's own acknowledgment of Hegseth's original classification authority is the substantive core of that defence and it is not empty - if he validly declassified the details before sending them, the classification-handling statutes are not engaged and only the policy violation remains. Trump publicly stood by Waltz, said he had 'learned a lesson', and Waltz was later moved to the UN ambassadorship rather than removed. Against the exoneration framing: the IG's finding of noncompliance with DoDI 8170.01 and of risk to pilots is a finding of fault on its own terms, and 'not classified' is not the same as 'appropriate'.
findings.status: IG finding of policy noncompliance; no charge, no referral, no discipline; Hegseth remained in office
findings.notes: Separately reported and not IG-adjudicated in this report: a second Signal chat in which Hegseth shared 15 March strike details including warplane flight schedules with his wife and brother. I tier that as labeled and did not verify it against a primary document. The brief asked whether an IG report exists - it does, and it is the single most substantive 2025-26 document on classified handling by this administration's principals.

findings.claim: On 1 April 2026 the DOJ Office of Legal Counsel, under Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser, issued a memorandum opinion for the Counsel to the President concluding that the Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and that 'the President need not further comply with its dictates', on the ground that the PRA 'is not a valid exercise of Congress's Article I authority and unconstitutionally intrudes on the independence and autonomy of the President guaranteed by Article II' and 'aggrandizes the legislative branch'. CREW, the Freedom of the Press Foundation and others sued; on 20 May 2026 the US District Court for the District of Columbia entered a preliminary injunction, effective 9:00 a.m. on 26 May 2026, requiring the White House Office, the National Security Council, the US DOGE Service and all advisers to the President to comply in full with the PRA, including preserving text and Signal messages, prohibiting the creation or sending of presidential records via ephemeral messaging without copying an official account, and requiring a compliance notice by 28 May 2026.
findings.legal_frame: 44 U.S.C. 2201-2209 (Presidential Records Act); U.S. Const. art. II (the OLC separation-of-powers theory); U.S. Const. art. I (the aggrandizement theory)
sources: CBS News, 'Justice Department says law requiring president to turn over records at end of administration is unconstitutional', https://www.cbsnews.com/news/justice-department-presidential-records-act-unconstitutional/
Washington Post, 'Justice Dept. says the Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional', 2 April 2026, https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/04/02/trump-doj-presidential-records-act/

NBC News, 'Justice Department says Trump does not have to turn over presidential records', https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/justice-department-says-trump-not-turn-presidential-records-rcna266434

CREW, 'Judge rules Trump White House must comply with Presidential Records Act', https://www.citizensforethics.org/news/press-releases/judge-rules-trump-white-house-must-comply-with-presidential-records-act/
Preliminary Injunction Order, D.D.C., 20 May 2026, https://www.historians.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/PI-Order.pdf (located; not fetched)

American Historical Association, 'Judge Grants Emergency Order Blocking Trump Administration from Disregarding Presidential Records Act', https://www.historians.org/news/judge-grants-emergency-order-blocking-trump-administration-from-disregarding-presidential-records-act/

CNN, 'Trump's DOJ tells Trump he can hold onto government docs when he leaves office', 3 April 2026, https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/03/politics/trump-presidential-records-act-watergate (HTTP 451 on fetch; not read directly)
findings.establishes: That the executive branch has now formally adopted, as a legal position, the proposition that the statute at the centre of the 2022 NARA referral does not bind the President - and that a federal court has preliminarily rejected it and ordered compliance.
findings.does_not: Establish that any records have in fact been destroyed or removed. A preliminary injunction is not a merits ruling; the case is at an early stage. The OLC opinion is an internal executive-branch legal position, not law, and binds no court.
findings.counter_record: The PRA's constitutionality under Article II has genuinely been questioned before this opinion, and the President's personal records - those of a 'purely private or nonpublic character' - are excluded from the Act by its own terms (44 U.S.C. 2201(3)). The government's position is that this is a separation-of-powers argument about the records of the presidency, not a licence to remove classified material, which is governed by entirely different statutes and would remain criminal regardless. That distinction is correct and important: nothing in the OLC opinion touches 18 U.S.C. 793 or 1924. Against that: the practical effect, as critics including CREW note, is to remove the civil recordkeeping framework whose 2022 operation generated the referral in the first place.
findings.status: under litigation; preliminary injunction against the government in force; no merits ruling
findings.notes: I did not read the OLC opinion itself and could not locate it on justice.gov; the quotations are as reported by CBS, NBC and the Washington Post. Tier the specific quoted phrases as labeled; the existence, date, author and holding are documented across three independent major outlets.

findings.claim: On 4 April 2024 Judge Cannon denied Trump's motion to dismiss the superseding indictment on Presidential Records Act grounds, rejecting the argument that a President may designate classified government records as 'personal' and lawfully retain them after leaving office. She noted that the charges 'make no reference to the Presidential Records Act' and do not rely on it for any charged offence.
sources: Washington Post, 'Judge Cannon shoots down Trump's Presidential Records Act claim', 4 April 2024, https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2024/04/04/cannon-trump-jack-smith-presidential-records-act/

NPR, 'Judge rules Trump's Mar-a-Lago classified documents case can proceed', 4 April 2024, https://www.npr.org/2024/04/04/1242897812/trump-classified-documents-mar-a-lago-jack-smith-judge-cannon-denied
CBS News, 'Judge denies Trump's motion to dismiss documents case', 4 April 2024, https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-documents-case-judge-denies-trumps-motion-to-dismiss/
findings.establishes: That the PRA 'personal records' defence was raised and rejected as a matter of law by the same judge who later dismissed the case on other grounds. It also establishes the correct legal frame: the case was never a Presidential Records Act case.
findings.does_not: Establish that Trump could not have prevailed on a related theory at trial, or that the classification/declassification defence was resolved - it was not. Cannon rejected the PRA dismissal argument but left related questions for trial, including jury instructions on the PRA, and never resolved them.
findings.counter_record: Cannon's denial was 'without prejudice' in substance - she declined to resolve the PRA's role as an evidentiary or instructional matter, and her earlier proposed jury instructions entertaining a version of the personal-records theory drew a sharp objection from the Special Counsel. The defence was never conclusively foreclosed on the merits.
findings.status: motion denied; case later dismissed on unrelated grounds
findings.notes: This finding exists to fix the legal frame. 793(e) does not require that information be classified. It protects information 'relating to the national defense' - a category that predates the modern classification system - and per CRS, classification marking is not an element, though courts defer to executive determinations of national-defense character (see Gorin v. United States, 312 U.S. 19 (1941), on the delimiting effect of the mens rea requirement). Consequence: a valid declassification would not by itself defeat a 793(e) count, and the declassification argument is therefore a weaker defence than it is usually described as being in public discussion. Source: CRS R41404, 'Criminal Prohibitions on Leaks and Other Disclosures of Classified Defense Information', https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R41404.

nulls.searched: Any charge, referral, indictment count, congressional referral, or court filing framing any of this conduct as treason - U.S. Const. art. III, sec. 3, or 18 U.S.C. 2381.
nulls.result: None found, anywhere, at any time. Not in the original indictment, not in the superseding indictment, not in Volume I of the Special Counsel report, not in Smith's December 2025 deposition or January 2026 testimony, not in Raskin's March 2026 letter, not in the DoD IG report. The Article III elements - levying war against the United States, or adhering to its enemies giving them aid and comfort, proved by two witnesses to the same overt act or confession in open court - are not engaged by any fact on this line. 'Enemies' in the clause has consistently been read to require a state of open war. No prosecutor has framed any of this under Article III. This is the most important null on the line and it should be published at equal prominence with everything above it.

nulls.searched: Any count under 18 U.S.C. 794 (gathering or delivering defense information to aid a foreign government) against Trump or any co-defendant.
nulls.result: None. 794 was never charged, never sought, and never referenced in any filing I located. 794 is the statute that carries life imprisonment or death and is the closest thing in US law to what people mean by 'treason' in the espionage context. Prosecutors with the Pratt reporting, the Bedminster recording, the PAC-representative map, and the January 2023 business-interest memo in hand charged 793(e) - a retention offence - and nothing more. That charging decision is a finding.

nulls.searched: Any count under 18 U.S.C. 798 (disclosure of classified communications intelligence), 18 U.S.C. 793(d) (transmission), 18 U.S.C. 1924 (unauthorized removal and retention by an officer or employee), 18 U.S.C. 2071 (concealment or removal of public records), or 42 U.S.C. 2274 (communication of Restricted Data).
nulls.result: None charged against Trump under any of them. On 1924: its text reaches an 'officer, employee, contractor, or consultant of the United States', and whether that includes a President is contested and was never litigated here. On 2071: it carries a disqualification-from-office clause whose applicability to the presidency is constitutionally doubtful under U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton, 514 U.S. 779 (1995), and it was not charged.

nulls.searched: Any conviction, acquittal, jury verdict, plea, or merits ruling on any classified-documents count against Trump.
nulls.result: None exists. Zero counts reached a jury. Zero counts were adjudicated on the merits by any court. The case ended three times over on grounds that touched no fact in the indictment: a structural Appointments Clause holding, an executive-branch policy against prosecuting a sitting President, and a discretionary dismissal by the succeeding administration. Anyone citing the ending of this case as evidence for or against the underlying conduct is running an unfalsifiable machine.

nulls.searched: The document Trump described on the July 2021 Bedminster recording - the Iran 'plan of attack'.
nulls.result: Never recovered. Trump's counsel searched and told the government they could not locate it. Its non-recovery is a real weakness in Count 32 and is part of the record.

nulls.searched: Any pardon, commutation, or clemency grant to Trump, Nauta or De Oliveira in the classified-documents matter.
nulls.result: None. The co-defendants' case was ended by DOJ motion, not clemency - reportedly a deliberate choice because a pardon implies wrongdoing to forgive. The guaranteed-null problem that a pardon would have created therefore does not arise on this line.

nulls.searched: Any evidence, in any source, that a classified US document retained at Mar-a-Lago or Bedminster reached a foreign government, foreign intelligence service, or foreign national.
nulls.result: None found. The January 2023 prosecution memo as quoted by Raskin raises the question and is redacted at exactly the point where an answer would appear. Raskin's eighth question to the Attorney General - whether any foreign actors accessed or attempted to access the documents - was, so far as I could find, not answered. This is an open question, not a finding, and must not be reported as one in either direction.

nulls.searched: The contents of Volume II of the Special Counsel's report.
nulls.result: Not public and not read by me. Sealed by court order since 21 January 2025, made permanent 23 February 2026, on appeal to the Eleventh Circuit as of 7 September 2026 with no merits ruling located. Guaranteed-null rule: the seal is evidence of nothing about the contents.

nulls.searched: Any finding, charge, or IG conclusion regarding President Trump personally in the March 2025 Signal episode.
nulls.result: None. He was not a participant in the chat. DODIG-2026-021 evaluated the Secretary of Defense, not the President. His documented involvement is that he publicly defended Waltz and Hegseth and imposed no discipline.

nulls.searched: Any 2025 or 2026 criminal investigation, grand jury, or charge against Trump relating to the handling of classified material.
nulls.result: None found. The 2025-26 activity on this line is entirely congressional oversight (Raskin's December 2025 and March 2026 letters, Smith's December 2025 deposition and January 2026 public testimony), civil records litigation (CREW/FPF v. Trump), and access litigation over Volume II. No criminal process is open against Trump on this subject.

nulls.searched: Any published damage assessment for the 10 May 2017 Lavrov/Kislyak disclosure or the 30 August 2019 satellite image.
nulls.result: None located for either. The Intelligence Community has never publicly quantified harm from either episode. Absent such an assessment, claims that either 'burned' a source or 'compromised' a capability are unsupported, and so are claims that neither caused harm.

nulls.result: Not extracted. The counts table in the scanned copy available to me is image-based and did not yield text; only fragments ('TOP SECRET//SPECIAL HANDLING'; a 4 June 2020 document 'concerning White House intelligence briefing... to various foreign countries') were legible. I do not assert a marking list. Anyone publishing one must go back to a text-layer copy of the indictment.

LEGAL FRAME, stated plainly because the brief asked for precision. This line contains no treason. Article III, sec. 3 requires levying war against the United States or adhering to its enemies giving them aid and comfort, with two witnesses to the same overt act or confession in open court, and 'enemies' means a power with which the United States is in a state of open war. Nothing in this record engages it, and no prosecutor, court or congressional referral has ever framed it that way. The correct frame for the Mar-a-Lago case is 18 U.S.C. 793(e) - willful retention of national defense information, an Espionage Act offence that requires neither espionage nor a foreign recipient nor intent to injure the United States. It is a retention crime. Charging 793(e) rather than 794 was the government's own considered judgment about what it could prove, and it is the single most probative fact in the record about the limits of the case.

THE DECLASSIFICATION COUNTER-ARGUMENT, which the brief flagged: it is real but narrower than usually described. A sitting President's authority over classification is constitutional (Department of the Navy v. Egan, 484 U.S. 518, 527 (1988)) and E.O. 13526 does not bind him. That defeats any criminal frame for the 2017 and 2019 episodes outright. It does much less work in the Mar-a-Lago case, for two reasons: 793(e) protects 'information relating to the national defense', a category that predates classification and does not require a classification marking as an element (CRS R41404; Gorin v. United States, 312 U.S. 19 (1941)); and the charged retention ran from 20 January 2021 onward, when Trump held no declassification authority at all. His own recorded words at Bedminster - 'as president I could have declassified it ... Now I can't' - state that distinction more clearly than any brief.

SYMMETRY. The strongest facts for the case are the audio recording, the 102 documents seized under a warrant after a certification of full production, and a prosecutor's on-the-record statement of proof beyond reasonable doubt. The strongest facts against it are that no jury ever heard any of it, that the government declined to charge on 305 of the 337 marked documents recovered, that it declined to charge transmission or any foreign-recipient offence despite having the Pratt account and the business-interest memo, that the Bedminster Iran document was never recovered, and that the prosecutor is now barred from producing the record that would let his claim be checked. Both sets are in the findings above and neither is discounted more than the other.
